messages.author: 0ab9f9b882fcbbb5
messages.subject: Removing outliers using outlie
parts:
Hey Chris,

I'm curious if you have a chunk of code that not only identifies outliers using the function "outlie" - but then removes those outliers from your data frame (my data frame was created using the as.telemetry function due to most of my data not being stored/coming from Movebank - rather, I receive .csv files from the data custodians I am collaborating with).

Thanks!

messages.author: 40fd627580dd34f5
messages.subject: Re: Removing outliers using outlie
parts:
Hi Ollie,

There is a simple example in the vignette('error') and in the ctmmlearn material. For datasets with a few outliers, I pluck them out as in the examples. For datasets with many outliers, I look at the different outputs from outlie() versus different error information in the data, like number of satellites or location class, and try to see if there is any pattern. I also look at the residuals of calibration data, if there are any. I plan to put in support for a heavy tailed error distribution at some point in the future to make that process a little more hands free.

Best,
Chris

Thanks for this, Chris. I do not have calibration data. How does that factor into error calibration?

Also, I ran the 'error' vignette. I noticed that the speed filter (i.e., BAD <- OUT$speed>0.08) somehow filtered out a single data point (the outlier) - yet that data points speed was 0.102..m/s while other data points i.e., 0.02138...m/s remained. If speed is meant to be > 0.08 then shouldn't 0.102 remain?

messages.author: 40fd627580dd34f5
messages.subject: Re: Removing outliers using outlie
parts:
Hi Ollie,

Calibration data helps estimate the error parameters and better identify predictors of outliers, as you know the tag/collar isn't moving.

You want to filter out things like biologically implausible speeds. A wood turtle can't really maintain 8cm/s over an extended period of time.

Best,
Chris

messages.author: 40fd627580dd34f5
messages.subject: Re: Removing outliers using outlie
parts:
Hi Ollie,

Yes, but before that I suggest running outlie() on all individuals to get a sense of the distribution of errors and what a good threshold might be.
You may also need to run a while() loop on each individual to keep running outlie() until there are no more outliers, in case there are sequential outliers.

Best,
Chris
